issues.legal_issue: A market committee’s representation structure is not an unreasonable restriction or unequal treatment merely because agricultural producers hold several seats.
material_facts: The committee had 23 members, of whom 10 represented producers.
Eight producer members were elected, and two producer members from scheduled castes were nominated to address the risk that they might otherwise lack representation.
The committee also included representatives of other interests and government officials.
issues.conclusion: The committee’s representation structure was not unreasonable, and the claim that producers had a perpetual majority was factually incorrect.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 14 and Article 19(1)(g) to the statutory representation scheme. It held that the representation of different interests, including producers who might otherwise lack representation, disclosed no unreasonable feature.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: Traders or other affected persons challenged the constitutionality of a regulated market scheme.
predicates.committee_has_no_producer_majority: The committee’s producer representatives do not form a majority of its membership.
predicates.committee_represents_diverse_interests: The committee includes representatives of multiple interests involved in the regulated activity, as well as public officials.

issues.definition: When a regulated market scheme is constitutionally challenged, a committee without a producer majority that represents diverse interests is not unreasonable on that account.

issues.legal_issue: Entrusting licensing decisions to a market committee representing different interests does not, without more, unreasonably restrict the right to trade.
material_facts: The challenged scheme assigned the licensing function to a market committee whose membership represented different interests in agricultural marketing and included government officials.
None of the petitioners had been refused a licence.
The scheme provided for appeals from committee decisions and further revision by the State Government, and the committee had to record reasons when refusing a licence.
issues.conclusion: Entrusting licensing to the committee did not make the scheme invalid or impose an unreasonable restriction on the right to trade.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 9(2), 13, 17, 25 and 32 of the Act, trading in the market yards required a licence; the committee could issue, renew, refuse, suspend or cancel licences, with appeals and revision available against its decisions. The Court held that a representative committee could exercise the licensing function properly and impartially, and that any mala fide or otherwise objectionable decision could be addressed in an individual case.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and licensing_is_decided_by_representative_committee and review_remedies_are_available and petitioners_have_no_refused_licence

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: Traders or other affected persons challenged the constitutionality of a regulated market scheme.
predicates.licensing_is_decided_by_representative_c: The scheme assigns licensing decisions to a committee representing different interests in the regulated trade.
predicates.review_remedies_are_available: A person affected by a licensing decision can seek review by an appellate or revisional authority.
predicates.petitioners_have_no_refused_licence: The persons bringing the challenge have not had their licence applications refused.

issues.definition: When licensing is assigned to a representative committee, review remedies are available, and the challengers have not been refused licences, the assignment is not unreasonable on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: Licensing criteria are not unconstitutionally vague when the scheme supplies adequate guidance for their application and constrains refusal decisions.
material_facts: The rules required an applicant to be solvent and a desirable person.
The Act stated the market scheme’s purposes and assigned the committee duties concerning fair dealings and enforcement of the Act and rules.
The application and licence forms set out relevant particulars and obligations.
The committee had to record reasons for refusing a licence, and its decisions were subject to appeal and revision.
issues.conclusion: The criteria, read with the guidance in the Act and rules and the procedural safeguards, were sufficiently guided and did not impose an unreasonable restriction.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 16, 17, 25 and 32 and rule 70(4)(i) supplied the relevant framework. Solvency was an intelligible criterion; the requirement that an applicant be a desirable or proper person was guided by the Act’s purposes, the committee’s duties, the application and licence forms, the duty to give reasons, and appeal and revision. The Court distinguished Lala Hari Chand Sarda v. Mizo District Council, where there was no appeal and no governing standard, and Harakchand Ratanchand Banthia v. Union of India, where the criteria lacked objective standards and the licensing scheme made the future of a business uncertain.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and licensing_uses_solvency_and_fitness_criteria and statutory_purpose_guides_decisions and refusal_requires_reasons and review_remedies_are_available

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: Traders or other affected persons challenged the constitutionality of a regulated market scheme.
predicates.licensing_uses_solvency_and_fitness_crit: The licensing authority assesses whether applicants are financially sound and fit to receive a licence.
predicates.statutory_purpose_guides_decisions: The governing scheme states purposes and duties that guide how the licensing authority assesses applicants.
predicates.refusal_requires_reasons: The licensing authority must state reasons when it refuses an application.
predicates.review_remedies_are_available: A person affected by a licensing decision can seek review by an appellate or revisional authority.

issues.definition: Licensing criteria are sufficiently guided when they assess solvency and fitness, the scheme’s purposes guide their application, refusals require reasons, and review is available.

issues.legal_issue: Requiring traders to provide storage pending adequate arrangements by the market committee is not an unreasonable restriction when storage is paid for.
material_facts: The scheme required the market committee to provide storage accommodation and facilities.
The traders’ storage obligation was treated as an interim measure pending the committee’s arrangements for proper storage.
Storage by traders in the market yards was subject to payment of a storage fee and other conditions specified in the applicable by-laws.
issues.conclusion: The storage requirement was not an unreasonable restriction on the traders’ right to trade.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(2)(vii) required the committee to provide storage accommodation, while rule 52(4) made storage subject to payment of a fee and conditions prescribed by by-laws. In that context, the traders’ storage role was interim and compensated.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: Traders or other affected persons challenged the constitutionality of a regulated market scheme.
predicates.traders_must_provide_interim_storage: The scheme requires traders to provide storage temporarily while the market authority arranges proper storage facilities.
predicates.storage_is_paid_for: The traders receive payment for storage under applicable market conditions.

issues.definition: A temporary requirement that traders provide storage is not unreasonable when the traders are paid for it.

issues.legal_issue: Requiring open-auction sales in regulated market yards is within the rule-making power and is not an unreasonable restriction on the right to trade.
material_facts: The rule required consignments of specified agricultural produce brought for sale into principal or sub-market yards to be sold by open auction, except for retail sales specified in the by-laws.
The Act authorized the making of rules to carry out its purposes and contemplated regulation of sale transactions in the market yards.
The Act’s licensing provisions, which restricted trading to licensed persons and made licences subject to rules, were not challenged.
The stated purpose of open auction was to help producers obtain the best price and reduce malpractices associated with private sales by individual negotiation.
issues.conclusion: The open-auction rule was within the rule-making power and did not violate the traders’ right to carry on business.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 9(2), 17 and 40, including section 40(2)(xxvii), supported the rule prescribing the mode of sale. The Court considered open auction a reasonable means of pursuing the Act’s purpose of securing the best price for producers and preventing malpractices; the retail-sale proviso limited the restriction. It distinguished Lala Hari Chand Sarda and Harakchand Ratanchand Banthia, which concerned different licensing defects and did not establish that this sale method was unreasonable.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and sale_rule_requires_open_auction and sale_method_is_within_rulemaking_authority and auction_advances_producer_protection and retail_sales_are_exempted

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: Traders or other affected persons challenged the constitutionality of a regulated market scheme.
predicates.sale_rule_requires_open_auction: A market rule requires goods brought for sale in regulated yards to be sold through open bidding.
predicates.sale_method_is_within_rulemaking_authori: The governing law authorizes rules to carry out the scheme’s purposes and to prescribe the mode of sale.
predicates.auction_advances_producer_protection: Open bidding is used to help producers obtain better prices and to reduce malpractices associated with private negotiation.
predicates.retail_sales_are_exempted: The rule does not apply its open-bidding requirement to specified retail sales.

issues.definition: An open-auction requirement is valid and reasonable when it is authorized, advances producer protection, and exempts specified retail sales.
